newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. wants more data about Iraq food distribution.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wants more data about Iraq food distribution.

text.p: American U.N. envoy Bill Richardson said Wednesday both Iraq and the U.N. secretariat needed to provide better information about the distribution of humanitarian goods under the "oil-for-food" deal.

He was speaking to reporters after the Security Council unanimously approved a six-month renewal of the scheme under which Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other necessities to help alleviate the effects of sanctions imposed after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

"We are not entirely satisfied with the implementation so far by the Iraqis and by the (U.N.) secretariat," Richardson said. "They need to provide better and more timely and accurate information, specifically on Iraq's distribution methods, the operation in the north, and other implementation facets that are not, in our judgment, being properly handled."

He was referring to measures, including on-the-spot U.N. monitoring, to ensure the fair distribution of humanitarian supplies among all sectors of the Iraqi population, both in the largely Kurdish-inhabited north of the country where the United Nations is in charge of distribution, and in the rest of the country , where Iraqi authorities are responsible, subject to U.N. monitoring.
Richardson added: "We don't have sufficient data. We think that the secretariat needs to provide more accurate data there. We think the Iraqis have been playing games with statistics, with figures.

"We feel that the main objective here is the humanitarian needs of the Iraqi people, and the Iraqi government doesn't seem to be concerned with that. They seem to be concerned with playing political games," he added.
Richardson said these issues would be "crucial in future decisions" regarding the "oil-for-food" deal.
The latest council resolution said the council would consider favourably a further renewal of the arrangement, provided it received satisfactory reports in the course of the next six months.
Asked about any increase in the $2 billion worth of oil sales permitted, he replied: "We don't think that's needed. We don't think an increase in oil sales is needed."
